title: Delivering Insights From a Food Delivery Marketplace
text: In a food delivery marketplace, the customer experience depends on much more than simply placing an order. Behind every completed transaction is a chain of coordinated actions involving restaurants, delivery partners, and the platform itself. This project examines that full lifecycle and shows how structured data can be used to evaluate both business performance and service quality.

title: Delivering Insights From a Food Delivery Marketplace
text:
🍔 From Order to Doorstep
This project explores the operational backbone of a digital food delivery marketplace. Using relational data across customers, restaurants, menu items, orders, and deliveries, I analyzed how the platform functions end to end and uncovered insights about customer spending, restaurant operations, courier efficiency, and delivery performance.

title: Delivering Insights From a Food Delivery Marketplace
text:
Business Context
Digital food delivery platforms operate as a two sided marketplace connecting customers with restaurants, while also relying on delivery partners to fulfill the final step of service. This makes them especially data rich and operationally complex.
The dataset represents the full journey of an order from the moment a customer browses the app to the point where food arrives at their doorstep. Because each entity is connected through a relational schema, the database makes it possible to evaluate both financial and operational outcomes across the platform.

What this database captures

Customer identity, activity, and location for segmentation and retention analysis
Restaurant supply, cuisine offerings, and menu level sales
Orders, fees, and transaction outcomes as the revenue engine of the platform
Delivery execution, including partner assignment, timing, and cost to serve

title: Delivering Insights From a Food Delivery Marketplace
text:
Why This Project Matters
This project goes beyond simple reporting. It reflects the types of business questions that matter in real marketplace environments.
For example:

Which customers generate the most value over time
Which restaurants or menu items are most profitable
Which delivery partners are most efficient
Where delays, bottlenecks, or quality issues may be affecting service

These questions sit at the intersection of analytics, operations, and strategy, making this a strong example of how data can be used to support decision making in a real business setting.

title: Delivering Insights From a Food Delivery Marketplace
text:
Database Structure and ERD
The schema is designed to model the full operational workflow of the marketplace.

Core entities
customers stores customer identity and location information, enabling segmentation and lifecycle analysis.
orders acts as the central transaction table and captures demand, revenue, fees, and fulfillment outcomes.
restaurants, menu_items, and order_items together represent the purchasing funnel, allowing analysis at both the restaurant and item level.
deliveries connects completed orders to delivery partners, making it possible to evaluate speed, reliability, and cost efficiency.


Core business processes supported

Customer acquisition and lifecycle management
Restaurant onboarding and menu publishing
Order placement and transaction processing
Item level sales and profitability analysis
Courier assignment and delivery execution
Marketplace coordination and service quality monitoring



ERD relationships

Customers (1,1) — (0,*) Orders
Each order belongs to exactly one customer, while a customer may place zero to many orders.
Delivery Partners (1,1) — (0,*) Deliveries Each delivery must be handled by exactly one driver, while a driver may complete zero to many deliveries.

title: Delivering Insights From a Food Delivery Marketplace
text:
Analytical Focus
My goal was to turn the relational structure of this database into actionable business insight. I approached the project through both SQL analysis and machine learning, using the database not just to answer static questions, but to understand how the marketplace behaves operationally.

title: Delivering Insights From a Food Delivery Marketplace
text: SQL Analysis and Business Insights

title: Delivering Insights From a Food Delivery Marketplace
text:
1. Delivery Partner Performance 🚴
One of the clearest operational questions was identifying which delivery partners were the fastest and which were the slowest.
Using SQL, I calculated average delivery times by partner and compared their performance across completed deliveries.

Key finding: Delivery speed varied clearly across delivery partners.

 
The fastest drivers, including Patty Holt, Shelley Lucas, and Bridget Summers, averaged roughly 22 to 23 minutes per delivery. On the other end, drivers such as Luke Peterson, Randy Kent, Joseph Lopez, and Martha Torres averaged closer to 27 minutes per delivery.
That roughly 5 minute gap is meaningful in a delivery marketplace. Even small delays can influence customer satisfaction, repeat ordering behavior, and perceptions of reliability.

Why this matters
This type of analysis can help a delivery platform:

identify high performing couriers
investigate operational inefficiencies
improve dispatching decisions
support service quality monitoring

title: Delivering Insights From a Food Delivery Marketplace
text:
2. Customer Spending and Delivery Economics 💳
Another question I explored was how much individual customers spend across the platform once delivery fees and tips are included.
This analysis required layered SQL logic and window functions to calculate the full cost of each customer’s orders over time. Rather than looking only at food subtotal, I focused on the broader contribution each customer makes to the delivery business model.

Key finding: Customer value is not just about order count, but also about total spend including fees and tips.

 
This matters because delivery platforms often earn a share of meal revenue while also benefiting from service fees and delivery charges. Customers who order frequently and spend more per transaction are especially valuable to long term marketplace profitability.

Business value of this analysis

supports customer segmentation
helps identify high value users
informs targeted retention or loyalty strategies
provides a clearer picture of lifetime value contribution

title: Delivering Insights From a Food Delivery Marketplace
text: Machine Learning Problem

title: Delivering Insights From a Food Delivery Marketplace
text:
Predicting Delivery Time ⏱️
To extend the project beyond descriptive analytics, I framed a machine learning problem around approximating delivery time.
Delivery time is a critical operational metric because it affects customer satisfaction, platform efficiency, and courier planning. I tested multiple regression based approaches to estimate how long a delivery would take and to understand which variables were most strongly associated with delays.



Entity Relationship Diagram



What I expected
Initially, I hypothesized that distance would be the strongest driver of delivery time.


What I found
Interestingly, the lasso regression results suggested something different. The variable with the strongest impact on longer delivery times was not distance, but being in Boston.

Unexpected insight: Geographic context appeared to matter more than raw distance alone.

This is likely due to omitted variable bias. The model did not include important real world factors such as traffic, road design, parking difficulty, and urban density, all of which can severely affect city deliveries.


Interpretation
This result reinforced an important lesson in analytics: the most intuitive variable is not always the most explanatory one. In real business settings, hidden operational complexity often shapes outcomes more than we initially expect.

title: Delivering Insights From a Food Delivery Marketplace
text:
Key Takeaways

Main insights from the project

Food delivery marketplaces can be analyzed as a full lifecycle system rather than a set of isolated transactions
SQL is highly effective for uncovering operational trends in courier performance and customer value
Small differences in delivery speed can have meaningful effects on customer experience
Delivery economics become more informative when fees and tips are included in customer spending analysis
Predictive modeling can reveal hidden drivers of performance, even when the model is imperfect

title: Delivering Insights From a Food Delivery Marketplace
text:
Limitations
No analysis is complete without acknowledging its limits.

Constraints in the dataset

Too many features made the model more generic and less interpretable
The data was not well segmented, which reduced prediction accuracy
The dataset covered only 10 months, so yearly seasonality could not be analyzed

title: Delivering Insights From a Food Delivery Marketplace
text:
Recommendations
Based on the findings, I would recommend expanding both the feature set and the segmentation strategy for future analysis.

Recommended next steps

Add features for time of day and day of week
Break the dataset into more homogeneous groups for stronger prediction accuracy
Build separate models for specific contexts, such as city based deliveries or bike only deliveries
Include operational variables such as traffic conditions and street layout where possible



Example of a stronger future prediction problem
Instead of predicting all deliveries at once, a more targeted model could estimate:
How long will a New York bike delivery take on a Friday night at 6 PM?
This type of narrower prediction would likely be much more useful for real operational planning and customer facing delivery estimates.

title: Delivering Insights From a Food Delivery Marketplace
text:
Final Reflection
This project demonstrates how structured relational data can be transformed into a business story. By combining database design, SQL analysis, and predictive modeling, I was able to explore how a digital marketplace operates across customers, restaurants, and couriers.
From identifying the fastest delivery partners to examining customer spending behavior and modeling delivery times, this work reflects the kind of analysis that supports real operational and strategic decisions.
For me, this project was especially valuable because it combined technical analytics with business context. It reinforced the idea that effective data analysis is not just about querying tables or building models. It is about understanding how systems work, where inefficiencies emerge, and how data can guide better decisions.

title: U.S. Job Market Analysis
text:
01 CLOUD ANALYTICS  PROJECT
        What can 1M+ job postings tell us about the future of data work?
        
          I analyzed real-world Lightcast job-market data to understand how data roles are evolving in the age of AI. From in-demand skills and salary differences to industry demand, experience requirements, and career pathways.
        

        
          Python
          PySpark
          AWS
          SQL
          Machine Learning
          Plotly
        
      

      
  

    

    
      RESEARCH QUESTIONS
      What did I want to understand?

      
        
          01 — SKILLS
          Which skills are most in demand?
          What are the most in-demand skills for data science, business analytics, and machine learning roles?
        

        
          02 — AI SHIFT
          Are job descriptions changing?
          Have job descriptions evolved in 2024 to require more AI and machine-learning expertise?
        

        
          03 — INDUSTRIES
          Where is hiring strongest?
          What industries are hiring the most data professionals, and where is demand concentrated?
        

        
          04 — CAREER
          What is the outlook for analytics?
          What do these market patterns suggest about the career outlook for business analytics professionals?
        
      
    


    
      02 RESEARCH RATIONALE
      Why study the changing boundaries between data roles?

      
        
          Data analyst work is increasingly moving beyond dashboards and traditional reporting toward deeper business context, automation, and responsibilities that overlap with data science, data engineering, and machine learning. At the same time, AI can automate many routine technical tasks, making the skill of being able to interpret data within a meaningful business context and translate analysis into decisions even more important.
        

        
          Three trends made this especially relevant in 2024: growing demand for AI and advanced analytics, increased emphasis on hybrid skill sets that combine tools such as Python and SQL with business communication, and clearer separation between traditional analytics positions and more specialized AI-focused roles. Remote and hybrid work have also expanded access to opportunities while increasing competition.
        

        
          I expected the market to reward both technical depth and business understanding, with noticeable differences in skills, experience, and compensation between traditional analytics and AI-oriented roles.
        
      
    


    
      03 SKILLS BY ROLE
      Which skills are employers looking for?
      
        Skill variables were processed independently to preserve the differences between software, specialized, common, and certification skill requirements. I cleaned the raw list fields, exploded them into individual observations, and ranked the most frequently occurring skills within each role category.
      

      
        
          
            Cleaning and extracting skills
            The code below is copied directly from my project notebook.
          
          PySpark
        

        
          
            
            Copy
          
          # clean and extract skills
from pyspark.sql.functions import regexp_replace, split, explode, trim, lower, col, lit

# clean the string and remove unwanted characters such as list brackets, quotes, and new lines
def extract_skills(dataframe, skill_col, skill_type):
    cleaned = dataframe.withColumn(
        "SKILL_CLEAN",
        regexp_replace(col(skill_col), r'[\[\]\n"]', "")
    )

# explode so its one row per skill and rename column
    exploded = cleaned.select(
        "ROLE_CATEGORY",
        explode(split(col("SKILL_CLEAN"), ",")).alias("SKILL")
    )

# clean formatting so everything is lower, trim any spaces, and remove empty values
    return exploded.withColumn(
        "SKILL",
        trim(lower(col("SKILL")))
    ).filter(
        (col("SKILL").isNotNull()) & (col("SKILL") != "")
    ).withColumn(
        "SKILL_TYPE",
        lit(skill_type)
    )
        
      

      
        
          
            Ranking the top skills by role
            I used a PySpark window function to identify the top 15 skills inside each role category.
          
          PySpark
        

        
          
            
            Copy
          
          # window function to extract and aggregate skill datasets to identify the top 15 most frequently occurring skills within each role category
from pyspark.sql.window import Window
from pyspark.sql.functions import col, row_number

def get_top_skills_by_role(df):
    counts = df.groupBy("ROLE_CATEGORY", "SKILL").count()

    window = Window.partitionBy("ROLE_CATEGORY").orderBy(col("count").desc())

    ranked = counts.withColumn(
        "rank",
        row_number().over(window)
    ).filter(col("rank") <= 15)

    return ranked
        
      

      Software skills


        
        
        


                            
                                            


      
        ✧   Key insight
        
          SQL, Python, and dashboarding tools appear consistently across all role categories, reinforcing them as foundational skills. Data Analyst postings lean more heavily on BI and reporting tools, while Data Scientist and AI-focused roles introduce a wider mix of programming, cloud, and machine-learning technologies.
        
      

      
        Additional skill analyses
        The same pipeline was applied to specialized skills, common soft skills, and certifications.

        Explore certifications

      04 MARKET INSIGHTS
      Salaries, industries, experience & work arrangements
      
        Skills are only one part of the market. I also compared compensation, industries, experience requirements, and work setup to understand how opportunities differ across data roles.
      

      
        
          AI ENGINEER
          $180K
          Median salary for AI Engineer/Analyst roles.
        
        
          DATA SCIENTIST
          $127.6K
          Median salary for Data Scientist roles.
        
        
          DATA ANALYST
          $97K
          Median salary for Data Analyst roles.
        
        
          EXPERIENCE
          39.6%
          of postings fell into the 3–5 year mid-level group.
        
      
      Salary comparison



                            
                                            


      Top industries hiring


                            
                                            


      Experience level distribution


                            
                                            


      Experience × work setup


                            
                                            


      
        ✧   Market insight
        
          Compensation rises with specialization: AI Engineer/Analyst roles had the highest median salary, followed by Data Scientists and Data Analysts. Hiring was concentrated in Finance & Insurance and Professional & Technical Services, while mid-level roles represented the largest experience group. Hybrid work dominated every experience level, with remote work consistently more common than onsite-only arrangements.
        
      
    


    
  05 UNSUPERVISED LEARNING

  
    
      Can job postings reveal natural career groupings without relying on job titles?

      
        Job titles are not always consistent across employers. I used K-Means clustering
        to explore whether data-related job postings would naturally form groups based
        on their underlying characteristics rather than their predefined role labels.
      

      
        K-Means is an unsupervised learning algorithm, so the model was not given a
        target variable to predict. Instead, it searched for similarity across salary,
        minimum experience, education, and feature engineered technical-skill indicators.
      
    

    
      MODEL
      K-Means
      Unsupervised clustering
      
        PySpark ML
        k = 4
        PCA
      
    
  


  
    MODEL PIPELINE
    From job postings to interpretable clusters

    
      
        
        01
        Filter
        Focus on relevant data roles
      

      →

      
        
        02
        Engineer
        Create binary skill indicators
      

      →

      
        
        03
        Scale
        Standardize model features
      

      →

      
        
        04
        Select k
        Compare WSSSE solutions
      

      →

      
        
        05
        Cluster
        Fit the K-Means model
      

      →

      
        
        06
        Interpret
        PCA + cluster profiles
      
    
  

  
    01 — FEATURE ENGINEERING
    How can job postings be represented by their technical skills?

    
     I first combined the available skill fields into a single text representation. I then converted the presence of selected technical skills into binary features (1 = present, 0 = absent), allowing each job posting’s skill profile to be represented numerically for clustering.
    

    
       Salary
       Experience
       Education
       Technical Skills
    

    
      
        
          
          PySpark
        
        # combine all skill text
from pyspark.sql.functions import concat_ws, coalesce, lit

skill_cols = [
    "SKILLS_NAME",
    "SPECIALIZED_SKILLS_NAME",
    "SOFTWARE_SKILLS_NAME",
    "COMMON_SKILLS_NAME"
]

df_roles = df_roles.withColumn(
    "ALL_SKILLS_TEXT",
    lower(
        concat_ws(
            " ",
            *[coalesce(col(c), lit("")) for c in skill_cols]
        )
    )
)
      

      
        
          
          PySpark
        
        # create binary skill features
from pyspark.sql.functions import regexp_extract

technical_skills = [
    "python","sql","excel","tableau","power bi",
    "machine learning","artificial intelligence",
    "data analysis","statistics","math",
    "linear algebra","probability","data visualization",
    "spark","aws","computer science"
]

df_skill_features = df_roles

for skill in technical_skills:
    clean_name = skill.replace(" ", "_").replace("-", "_").replace("/", "_")
    pattern = rf"\\b{skill.lower()}\\b"
    
    df_skill_features = df_skill_features.withColumn(
        f"skill_{clean_name}",
        (regexp_extract(col("ALL_SKILLS_TEXT"), pattern, 0) != "").cast("int")
    )
      
    
  


  
    02 — PREPARING FEATURES FOR CLUSTERING
    Preparing the skill profiles for K-Means

    
      After creating the binary skill indicators, I combined salary, minimum experience,
      education level, and the engineered skill variables into a single feature vector.
      PySpark's K-Means implementation expects the model inputs in this vector format.
      I then standardized the vector before applying the distance-based clustering model.
    
    
    
      
      
        Why standardize?
        
          K-Means groups observations using distance. Salary, experience, education,
          and binary skill indicators are measured on different numerical scales, so
          standardization keeps a high-magnitude variable such as salary from dominating
          the distance calculation simply because of its units.
        
      
    
  


  
    03 — CHOOSING THE NUMBER OF CLUSTERS
    How many groups best represent the job market?

    
      I trained candidate K-Means models for k = 2, 3, and 4 and compared their
      within-cluster sum of squared errors (WSSSE). Lower WSSSE means observations
      sit closer to their assigned cluster centers. The error continued to decline
      across the tested values, but the curve did not show a sharp elbow.
    

    
      
        
          
          PySpark ML
        
        # compare candidate values of k
cost = []
k_values = range(2, 5)

for k in k_values:
    kmeans = KMeans(
        k=k,
        featuresCol="scaled_features",
        seed=42
    )
    model = kmeans.fit(df_model)
    cost.append(model.summary.trainingCost)
      

      
        
        Elbow-method comparison. WSSSE falls from k = 2 through k = 4 without a dramatic bend, so the plot does not identify one unambiguous cluster count.
      
    

    
      4
      
        SELECTED CLUSTER COUNT
        Why k = 4?
        
          I selected four clusters as an exploratory balance between additional
          segmentation and interpretability. Because the tested WSSSE curve does not
          contain a dramatic elbow, I do not treat four as the single “true” number
          of occupational groups; instead, I use it as a useful structure for examining
          different skill and job profiles.
        
      
    
  


  
    04 — K-MEANS CLUSTERING

    
      
        Grouping postings by technical skill profile
        Using the selected k = 4, I fit the final model on the standardized feature vectors and assigned each posting to its nearest cluster centroid.
      
      PySpark ML
    

    
      
        
      
      # fit the selected four-cluster solution
kmeans = KMeans(k=4, featuresCol="scaled_features", seed=42)
model = kmeans.fit(df_model)
df_clustered = model.transform(df_model)
    
  


  
    05 — INTERPRETING THE CLUSTERS
    What makes each cluster different?

    
      I profiled each cluster by examining its dominant skills and broader job
      characteristics. The resulting groups were interpretable, but they represented
      different levels and types of specialization rather than four perfectly isolated
      occupations.
    

    
      
        C0
        
          PROFILE
          Traditional Analytics
          SQL-heavy analytical work with less emphasis on advanced ML and statistical skills.
        
      

      
        C1
        
          PROFILE
          Data Science
          Greater emphasis on machine learning, statistics, probability, and quantitative depth.
        
      

      
        C2
        
          PROFILE
          Generalist / Mixed
          A more heterogeneous group with weaker concentration around one technical specialty.
        
      

      
        C3
        
          PROFILE
          Business Intelligence
          Strong SQL combined with BI, dashboarding, and visualization-oriented tools.
        
      
    

    
      
      
    

    
      Cluster 1Shows the broadest technical profile, with strong SQL, data analysis, Tableau, Power BI, Python, visualization, and statistics presence.
      Cluster 3Is strongly anchored by SQL and data analysis, but has much lower presence of the broader BI and advanced technical skills.
      Across clustersThe groups differ mainly in skill combinations and intensity rather than completely exclusive skill sets.
    
  


  
    06 — PCA VISUALIZATION
    How distinct are the clusters in a lower-dimensional view?

    
      I used Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to project the high-dimensional
      model features into two dimensions. This makes the cluster structure easier
      to inspect visually, although PCA necessarily compresses information from the
      original feature space.
    

    
      

      
        
        PCA view of the four-cluster solution. The colors overlap substantially rather than forming four isolated clouds, reinforcing that the underlying job profiles share many characteristics.
      
    

    
      KEY MODEL FINDING
      Data careers appear to exist on a spectrum.
      
        The elbow curve, cluster skill profiles, and PCA view tell a consistent story:
        meaningful differences in skill composition exist, but the boundaries are not
        rigid. Traditional analytics, BI, data science, and AI-oriented postings share
        many underlying capabilities and differ more by combinations and depth of skills
        than by completely separate occupational categories.
      
    
  


  
    06 — CONCLUSION 
    MODEL LIMITATIONS & NEXT TESTS

    
      
      
        Clustering is exploratory, not ground truth.
        
          K-Means assumes distance-based, relatively compact clusters. The gradual
          WSSSE curve and PCA overlap indicate that this labor-market data does not
          naturally divide into sharply separated groups. PCA also compresses the
          full feature space into two dimensions, so some structure can be lost in
          visualization.
        
        
          If I extended the model, I would test a wider range of k values using
          silhouette scores, compare cluster membership against the original role
          categories, and evaluate cluster stability across several random seeds.
          Those checks would help determine whether the observed groupings are
          consistently reproducible or primarily exploratory.
        
      
    
  



    
      06 LITERATURE REVIEW
      Do the findings align with other labor-market research?

      
        Skills-based hiring & hybrid skill sets

        
          Kobets et al. (2024) analyzed 3,744 job postings and used K-means clustering to identify four data-role groupings: Data Analyst & Engineer, Data Platform Engineer, Data Science & Engineering Specialist, and Cloud Data Engineer. Their results similarly suggest that modern data roles are increasingly defined by combinations of competencies rather than job titles alone.
        

        
          The study highlights Python, SQL, cloud platforms such as AWS and Azure, data engineering, analytics, and machine learning as recurring requirements. It also identifies a gap between academic training and industry needs, reinforcing the importance of continuous upskilling and hybrid technical/business skill sets.
        

        
          This provides useful external support for the patterns in my own analysis: SQL and Python function as core skills, specialized tools distinguish different career paths, and skill composition often provides a clearer picture of role structure than title alone.
        

        
          Reference:
          
            Kobets, Gulin, and Nosov (2024)

I cleaned the raw list fields, exploded them into individual observations, and ranked the most frequently occurring skills within each role category.
      

      
        
          
            Cleaning and extracting skills
            The code below is copied directly from my project notebook.
          
          PySpark
        

        
          
            
            Copy
          
          # clean and extract skills
from pyspark.sql.functions import regexp_replace, split, explode, trim, lower, col, lit

# clean the string and remove unwanted characters such as list brackets, quotes, and new lines
def extract_skills(dataframe, skill_col, skill_type):
    cleaned = dataframe.withColumn(
        "SKILL_CLEAN",
        regexp_replace(col(skill_col), r'[\[\]\n"]', "")
    )

# explode so its one row per skill and rename column
    exploded = cleaned.select(
        "ROLE_CATEGORY",
        explode(split(col("SKILL_CLEAN"), ",")).alias("SKILL")
    )

# clean formatting so everything is lower, trim any spaces, and remove empty values
    return exploded.withColumn(
        "SKILL",
        trim(lower(col("SKILL")))
    ).filter(
        (col("SKILL").isNotNull()) & (col("SKILL") != "")
    ).withColumn(
        "SKILL_TYPE",
        lit(skill_type)
    )
        
      

      
        
          
            Ranking the top skills by role
            I used a PySpark window function to identify the top 15 skills inside each role category.
          
          PySpark
        

        
          
            
            Copy
          
          # window function to extract and aggregate skill datasets to identify the top 15 most frequently occurring skills within each role category
from pyspark.sql.window import Window
from pyspark.sql.functions import col, row_number

def get_top_skills_by_role(df):
    counts = df.groupBy("ROLE_CATEGORY", "SKILL").count()

    window = Window.partitionBy("ROLE_CATEGORY").orderBy(col("count").desc())

    ranked = counts.withColumn(
        "rank",
        row_number().over(window)
    ).filter(col("rank") <= 15)

    return ranked

      05 UNSUPERVISED LEARNING: K-MEANS CLUSTERING
      Can the job market reveal natural role groupings without relying on job titles?
      
        Because job titles are inconsistent across employers, I used unsupervised machine learning to test whether postings would naturally group together based on underlying skills, salary, experience, and education without relying on predefined job titles.

      07 LITERATURE REVIEW
      Do the findings align with other labor-market research?

      
        Skills-based hiring & hybrid skill sets

        
          Kobets et al. (2024) analyzed 3,744 job postings and used K-means clustering to identify four data-role groupings: Data Analyst & Engineer, Data Platform Engineer, Data Science & Engineering Specialist, and Cloud Data Engineer. Their results similarly suggest that modern data roles are increasingly defined by combinations of competencies rather than job titles alone.
        

        
          The study highlights Python, SQL, cloud platforms such as AWS and Azure, data engineering, analytics, and machine learning as recurring requirements. It also identifies a gap between academic training and industry needs, reinforcing the importance of continuous upskilling and hybrid technical/business skill sets.

title: Projects
About
Delivering Insights From a Food Delivery Marketplace
text: In a food delivery marketplace, the customer experience depends on much more than simply placing an order. Behind every completed transaction is a chain of coordinated actions involving restaurants, delivery partners, and the platform itself. This project examines that full lifecycle and shows how structured data can be used to evaluate both business performance and service quality.

title: Delivering Insights From a Food Delivery Marketplace
text:
🍔 From Order to Doorstep
This project explores the operational backbone of a digital food delivery marketplace. Using relational data across customers, restaurants, menu items, orders, and deliveries, I analyzed how the platform functions end to end and uncovered insights about customer spending, restaurant operations, courier efficiency, and delivery performance.

title: Delivering Insights From a Food Delivery Marketplace
text:
Business Context
Digital food delivery platforms operate as a two sided marketplace connecting customers with restaurants, while also relying on delivery partners to fulfill the final step of service. This makes them especially data rich and operationally complex.
The dataset represents the full journey of an order from the moment a customer browses the app to the point where food arrives at their doorstep. Because each entity is connected through a relational schema, the database makes it possible to evaluate both financial and operational outcomes across the platform.

What this database captures

Customer identity, activity, and location for segmentation and retention analysis
Restaurant supply, cuisine offerings, and menu level sales
Orders, fees, and transaction outcomes as the revenue engine of the platform
Delivery execution, including partner assignment, timing, and cost to serve

title: Delivering Insights From a Food Delivery Marketplace
text:
Why This Project Matters
This project goes beyond simple reporting. It reflects the types of business questions that matter in real marketplace environments.
For example:

Which customers generate the most value over time
Which restaurants or menu items are most profitable
Which delivery partners are most efficient
Where delays, bottlenecks, or quality issues may be affecting service

These questions sit at the intersection of analytics, operations, and strategy, making this a strong example of how data can be used to support decision making in a real business setting.

title: Delivering Insights From a Food Delivery Marketplace
text:
Database Structure and ERD
The schema is designed to model the full operational workflow of the marketplace.

Core entities
customers stores customer identity and location information, enabling segmentation and lifecycle analysis.
orders acts as the central transaction table and captures demand, revenue, fees, and fulfillment outcomes.
restaurants, menu_items, and order_items together represent the purchasing funnel, allowing analysis at both the restaurant and item level.
deliveries connects completed orders to delivery partners, making it possible to evaluate speed, reliability, and cost efficiency.


Core business processes supported

Customer acquisition and lifecycle management
Restaurant onboarding and menu publishing
Order placement and transaction processing
Item level sales and profitability analysis
Courier assignment and delivery execution
Marketplace coordination and service quality monitoring



ERD relationships

Customers (1,1) — (0,*) Orders
Each order belongs to exactly one customer, while a customer may place zero to many orders.
Delivery Partners (1,1) — (0,*) Deliveries Each delivery must be handled by exactly one driver, while a driver may complete zero to many deliveries.

title: Delivering Insights From a Food Delivery Marketplace
text:
Analytical Focus
My goal was to turn the relational structure of this database into actionable business insight. I approached the project through both SQL analysis and machine learning, using the database not just to answer static questions, but to understand how the marketplace behaves operationally.

title: Delivering Insights From a Food Delivery Marketplace
text: SQL Analysis and Business Insights

title: Delivering Insights From a Food Delivery Marketplace
text:
1. Delivery Partner Performance 🚴
One of the clearest operational questions was identifying which delivery partners were the fastest and which were the slowest.
Using SQL, I calculated average delivery times by partner and compared their performance across completed deliveries.

Key finding: Delivery speed varied clearly across delivery partners.

 
The fastest drivers, including Patty Holt, Shelley Lucas, and Bridget Summers, averaged roughly 22 to 23 minutes per delivery. On the other end, drivers such as Luke Peterson, Randy Kent, Joseph Lopez, and Martha Torres averaged closer to 27 minutes per delivery.
That roughly 5 minute gap is meaningful in a delivery marketplace. Even small delays can influence customer satisfaction, repeat ordering behavior, and perceptions of reliability.

Why this matters
This type of analysis can help a delivery platform:

identify high performing couriers
investigate operational inefficiencies
improve dispatching decisions
support service quality monitoring

title: Delivering Insights From a Food Delivery Marketplace
text:
2. Customer Spending and Delivery Economics 💳
Another question I explored was how much individual customers spend across the platform once delivery fees and tips are included.
This analysis required layered SQL logic and window functions to calculate the full cost of each customer’s orders over time. Rather than looking only at food subtotal, I focused on the broader contribution each customer makes to the delivery business model.

Key finding: Customer value is not just about order count, but also about total spend including fees and tips.

 
This matters because delivery platforms often earn a share of meal revenue while also benefiting from service fees and delivery charges. Customers who order frequently and spend more per transaction are especially valuable to long term marketplace profitability.

Business value of this analysis

supports customer segmentation
helps identify high value users
informs targeted retention or loyalty strategies
provides a clearer picture of lifetime value contribution

title: Delivering Insights From a Food Delivery Marketplace
text: Machine Learning Problem

title: Delivering Insights From a Food Delivery Marketplace
text:
Predicting Delivery Time ⏱️
To extend the project beyond descriptive analytics, I framed a machine learning problem around approximating delivery time.
Delivery time is a critical operational metric because it affects customer satisfaction, platform efficiency, and courier planning. I tested multiple regression based approaches to estimate how long a delivery would take and to understand which variables were most strongly associated with delays.



Entity Relationship Diagram



What I expected
Initially, I hypothesized that distance would be the strongest driver of delivery time.


What I found
Interestingly, the lasso regression results suggested something different. The variable with the strongest impact on longer delivery times was not distance, but being in Boston.

Unexpected insight: Geographic context appeared to matter more than raw distance alone.

This is likely due to omitted variable bias. The model did not include important real world factors such as traffic, road design, parking difficulty, and urban density, all of which can severely affect city deliveries.


Interpretation
This result reinforced an important lesson in analytics: the most intuitive variable is not always the most explanatory one. In real business settings, hidden operational complexity often shapes outcomes more than we initially expect.

title: Delivering Insights From a Food Delivery Marketplace
text:
Key Takeaways

Main insights from the project

Food delivery marketplaces can be analyzed as a full lifecycle system rather than a set of isolated transactions
SQL is highly effective for uncovering operational trends in courier performance and customer value
Small differences in delivery speed can have meaningful effects on customer experience
Delivery economics become more informative when fees and tips are included in customer spending analysis
Predictive modeling can reveal hidden drivers of performance, even when the model is imperfect

title: Delivering Insights From a Food Delivery Marketplace
text:
Limitations
No analysis is complete without acknowledging its limits.

Constraints in the dataset

Too many features made the model more generic and less interpretable
The data was not well segmented, which reduced prediction accuracy
The dataset covered only 10 months, so yearly seasonality could not be analyzed

title: Delivering Insights From a Food Delivery Marketplace
text:
Recommendations
Based on the findings, I would recommend expanding both the feature set and the segmentation strategy for future analysis.

Recommended next steps

Add features for time of day and day of week
Break the dataset into more homogeneous groups for stronger prediction accuracy
Build separate models for specific contexts, such as city based deliveries or bike only deliveries
Include operational variables such as traffic conditions and street layout where possible



Example of a stronger future prediction problem
Instead of predicting all deliveries at once, a more targeted model could estimate:
How long will a New York bike delivery take on a Friday night at 6 PM?
This type of narrower prediction would likely be much more useful for real operational planning and customer facing delivery estimates.

title: Delivering Insights From a Food Delivery Marketplace
text:
Final Reflection
This project demonstrates how structured relational data can be transformed into a business story. By combining database design, SQL analysis, and predictive modeling, I was able to explore how a digital marketplace operates across customers, restaurants, and couriers.
From identifying the fastest delivery partners to examining customer spending behavior and modeling delivery times, this work reflects the kind of analysis that supports real operational and strategic decisions.
For me, this project was especially valuable because it combined technical analytics with business context. It reinforced the idea that effective data analysis is not just about querying tables or building models. It is about understanding how systems work, where inefficiencies emerge, and how data can guide better decisions.

      PROJECT QUESTIONS

        03 — HOST QUALITYHow does hosting quality vary?Explore superhost concentration and whether high-demand central areas show more professionalized hosting.
        04 — MACHINE LEARNINGCan models reveal useful listing patterns?Test classification, transformer-based text modeling, and clustering on different aspects of the Zurich market.
      
    

    
      02 PROCESSING & CLEANING
      Preparing a messy marketplace dataset for analysis
      
        I treated missing values based on the meaning of each variable rather than applying one
        blanket imputation rule. Missing bathrooms, bedrooms, and beds were inferred using related
        listing information such as guest capacity; host response variables were cleaned and encoded;
        extreme bed and bedroom values were handled before modeling; text nulls were converted to
        empty strings for compatibility; and low-information or heavily missing fields were removed.

      What do listing characteristics tell us about the market?

      
        ROOM TYPE
        Entire homes dominate many high-demand areas
        
          
            Entire homes and apartments make up much of the supply across Zurich. The presentation notes that central areas such as Langstrasse, Seefeld, and Altstadt show more entire-home rentals, while private and shared rooms appear more often in select peripheral areas.
          
          Room type distribution by neighborhood.
        
      

      
        HOST QUALITY
        Superhost concentration varies substantially by neighborhood
        
          
            Central, tourism-heavy, and higher-demand neighborhoods show stronger superhost concentrations in the analysis, suggesting that competitive markets may push hosts toward more professional service standards.
          
          Percentage of superhosts by neighborhood.
        
      

      
        PRICE & CAPACITY
        Larger listings tend to cost more — but size is not the whole story
        
          
            The analysis finds a positive relationship between guest capacity and price, alongside substantial price variation at each capacity level. Location, amenities, room type, and property quality therefore appear important alongside size.

      05 MACHINE LEARNING
      Testing structured and unstructured approaches
      
        KNN CLASSIFICATIONParking availabilityUsed accommodates, bathrooms, bedrooms, beds, and price to classify whether a listing offered parking. The reported accuracy was 0.58 versus a 0.53 naive baseline.
        TRANSFORMERPrice quartile from textFine-tuned DistilBERT on listing description, host_about, and amenities to predict price quartile. The presentation reports validation accuracy around 0.442.

      KNN classification: parking availability was only modestly predictable from the selected listing features.
      DistilBERT experiment: listing text captured some pricing signal, but the presentation notes limited improvement with additional training.
    

    
      06 CLUSTERING ANALYSIS
      Segmenting Zurich listings into five market profiles
      
        The K-Means analysis grouped listings using price, guest capacity, review volume,
        review score, and 30-day booking demand. The selected five-cluster solution was
        used to describe listing segments ranging from budget/high-occupancy supply to
        premium large-capacity listings.
      

      The project selected five clusters after comparing K-Means inertia and balancing segmentation with interpretability.
      Cluster-level comparisons show meaningful differences in average price, demand, and listing counts.

      
        What the clustering adds
        Rather than treating Zurich as one homogeneous Airbnb market, the segmentation reveals distinct combinations of price, capacity, popularity, and demand — useful for thinking about positioning and market strategy.
      
    

    
      07 KEY TAKEAWAYS
      What did the analysis suggest?

        PRICINGSize helps, but does not explain everythingCapacity is positively related to price, but location, room type, amenities, and listing quality also contribute to the spread.
        DEMANDShort-term demand is unevenBooking activity differs across neighborhoods, with some central areas showing substantially stronger near-term demand.
        LISTINGSEntire homes dominateThe Zurich market is heavily oriented toward entire-home rentals, particularly in central and higher-demand areas.
        MODELINGPredictive signal was mixedKNN and transformer experiments found some signal, but neither selected feature set fully explained the target outcomes.

Model interpretation
The target is close to balanced, so the 0.58 accuracy is not being created by an overwhelmingly dominant class. Precision, recall, and F1 are also fairly even across the two classes, but all remain around the high-0.50 range. This means the model is not reliably separating listings with parking from listings without parking.


Key takeaway
Parking availability is not strongly explained by accommodates, bathrooms, bedrooms, beds, and price alone. Location, property type, and richer amenity information may carry more useful signal and would be natural additions in a stronger model.

title: Delivering Insights From a Food Delivery Marketplace
text:
01 DATABASE + ANALYTICS PROJECT
    What happens between placing an order and food arriving at the doorstep?
    I analyzed the operational backbone of a digital food delivery marketplace using relational data across customers, restaurants, menu items, orders, couriers, and deliveries. The goal was to understand how the platform performs end to end — from customer spending to delivery efficiency.
    
      SQLSQLiteRelational DatabasesERDRegressionBusiness Analytics
    
  
  🍔



  BUSINESS QUESTIONS
  What did I want to understand?
  
    01 — CUSTOMERSWho creates the most value?Which customers contribute the most total spend once food, delivery fees, and tips are considered together?
    02 — RESTAURANTSWhat drives marketplace sales?How can restaurant, menu, order, and item-level data be connected to understand purchasing activity?
    03 — COURIERSWho delivers most efficiently?Which delivery partners are fastest, where do performance gaps appear, and what could those gaps mean operationally?
    04 — PREDICTIONWhat explains delivery time?Can regression help approximate delivery duration and reveal which features are most associated with delays?
  



  02 DATABASE STRUCTURE
  Modeling the full order lifecycle
  The relational schema connects the customer experience to the operational work happening behind the scenes. Customers place orders, restaurants publish menu items, order items capture the products purchased, and deliveries connect fulfilled orders to delivery partners.
  
    CUSTOMERSDemandIdentity, activity, and location support segmentation and lifecycle analysis.
    ORDERSTransactionsThe central transaction table captures demand, fees, revenue, and fulfillment outcomes.
    RESTAURANTSSupplyRestaurants, menu items, and order items represent the purchasing funnel.
    DELIVERIESFulfillmentCourier assignment, pickup/drop-off timing, tips, and cost connect operations to service quality.
  
  
    Key relationships. Each order belongs to exactly one customer, while a customer can place zero to many orders. Each delivery is handled by exactly one delivery partner, while a partner can complete zero to many deliveries. Together, the schema supports analysis across customer acquisition, restaurant supply, transaction processing, item-level sales, courier execution, and marketplace service quality.
  



  03 SQL ANALYSIS
  Turning relational data into business insight
  I used SQL joins, aggregations, date calculations, CTEs, and grouped analysis to move beyond individual tables and evaluate how the marketplace behaves as a connected system.
  
    OPERATIONSCourier performanceCompare average delivery time and completed delivery volume across delivery partners.
    CUSTOMER VALUETotal platform spendCombine item totals, delivery fees, and tips to calculate broader customer contribution.
    DECISION SUPPORTActionable outputTranslate query results into questions about dispatching, retention, and service quality.
  



  04 DELIVERY PARTNER PERFORMANCE
  How much does delivery speed vary by courier?
  One of the clearest operational questions was identifying the fastest and slowest delivery partners. I calculated average delivery time from pickup to drop-off and compared performance across completed deliveries.
  Average delivery time by partnerThe query calculates delivery duration in minutes and ranks partners from fastest to slowest.SQL
  CopySELECT
    dp.dp_id,
    dp.name,
    ROUND(
        AVG((julianday(d.dropoff_time) - julianday(d.pickup_time)) * 24 * 60),
        2
    ) AS avg_delivery_minutes,
    COUNT(d.delivery_id) AS total_deliveries
FROM delivery_partners dp
JOIN deliveries d ON dp.dp_id = d.dp_id
WHERE d.pickup_time IS NOT NULL
  AND d.dropoff_time IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY dp.dp_id, dp.name
ORDER BY avg_delivery_minutes ASC;
  ✦   Key findingDelivery speed varied clearly across partners. Patty Holt, Shelley Lucas, and Bridget Summers averaged roughly 22–23 minutes per delivery, while Luke Peterson, Randy Kent, Joseph Lopez, and Martha Torres were closer to 27 minutes — a gap of about five minutes.
  Why this matters. Even a relatively small delivery-time gap can influence customer satisfaction, repeat ordering, and perceptions of reliability. This analysis can help identify high-performing couriers, investigate inefficiencies, improve dispatching decisions, and monitor service quality.



  05 CUSTOMER SPENDING
  Customer value is more than order count
  To understand customer contribution, I calculated the full cost of each customer's orders rather than looking only at food subtotal. The analysis combines item prices and quantities with delivery fees and tips.
  Building total customer spendLayered CTEs connect order items, orders, and deliveries before aggregating to the customer level.SQL
  CopyWITH customer_payment_info AS (
    WITH order_price_info AS (
        SELECT
            oi.item_price_at_order,
            oi.quantity,
            oi.order_id,
            o.customer_id,
            d.tip_amount,
            o.delivery_fee
        FROM order_items oi
        LEFT JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
        LEFT JOIN deliveries d ON oi.order_id = d.order_id
    )
    SELECT
        customer_id,
        tip_amount,
        delivery_fee,
        SUM(item_price_at_order * quantity) AS order_total
    FROM order_price_info
    GROUP BY order_id
)
SELECT
    customer_id,
    SUM(tip_amount + delivery_fee + order_total) AS customer_total
FROM customer_payment_info
GROUP BY customer_id
ORDER BY customer_id;
  ✦   Key findingCustomer value is not just about how often someone orders. Total spend becomes more informative when the food subtotal, delivery fee, and tip are considered together.
  
    01SegmentGroup customers using broader spending behavior.
    02IdentifySurface high-value users across the marketplace.
    03RetainInform targeted loyalty and retention strategies.
    04MeasureBuild a clearer picture of lifetime value contribution.
  



  06 MACHINE LEARNING
  
    Predicting delivery timeI extended the project beyond descriptive analytics by framing a regression problem around delivery duration. The goal was to approximate how long a delivery would take and understand which variables were most strongly associated with delays.
    MODELLassoRegression with standardized featuresDelivery timeGeographyDistanceOperations
  
  
    EXPECTATIONDistanceI initially expected distance to be the strongest driver of delivery time.
    RESULTBostonThe strongest positive coefficient was associated with being in Boston rather than raw distance.
    INTERPRETATIONContext mattersGeographic context appeared to capture operational complexity that distance alone did not explain.
  
  ↗Unexpected insightGeographic context appeared to matter more than raw distance alone. A likely explanation is omitted-variable bias: traffic, road design, parking difficulty, and urban density were not represented directly in the model.
  This reinforced an important analytics lesson: the most intuitive variable is not always the most explanatory one. In operational settings, hidden complexity can shape outcomes more than a simple measure such as distance.



  07 TAKEAWAYS
  What I learned from the marketplace
  
    01 — SYSTEM VIEWAnalyze the full lifecycleFood delivery is better understood as a connected system than as isolated transactions.
    02 — SQLOperational patterns emergeRelational analysis makes courier performance and customer value measurable across entities.
    03 — MODELINGPrediction exposes hidden driversEven an imperfect model can reveal factors that deserve deeper operational investigation.
  

  LimitationsThe model and dataset leave room for more targeted future analysis.
  
    DATA10 monthsThe dataset was too short to evaluate full-year seasonality.
    FEATURESToo broadToo many features made the model more generic and less interpretable.
    SEGMENTSMixed contextsInsufficient segmentation reduced prediction accuracy.
    OPERATIONSMissing contextTraffic, street layout, parking, and density were not directly modeled.
  

  Recommended next stepsFuture modeling should narrow the prediction context and add operational features.
  Add time-of-day and day-of-week features, segment deliveries into more homogeneous groups, build context-specific models such as city-based or bike-only deliveries, and incorporate traffic or street-layout variables where possible. A stronger future question would be: How long will a New York bike delivery take on a Friday night at 6 PM?

  Final reflectionThis project showed me how structured relational data can be transformed into a business story. Combining database design, SQL analysis, and predictive modeling made it possible to examine the marketplace across customers, restaurants, and couriers — and connect technical analysis back to operational decisions.
